name: Aaron Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a junior operator on a wire-drawing machine that makes steel bicycle spokes. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check tension after a guide wheel change. I enjoy watching a clean spool wind evenly; a broken wire under tension makes the restart tiring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are home, pay and AI use like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner enters invoices for a plumbing supplier, and we have two school-age children, eight and fourteen, and a mortgage. I earn typical factory pay; we have four months of expenses saved and some similar plants nearby. I use AI now and then for fault-code words, but verify against the manual and measured spokes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the wire room that AI can sort an invoice faster, but a bicycle spoke still has to come off the drawing die at the right diameter. A thin spoke is not fixed by a better spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My machine wage is the usual rate, my partner's invoice job is steady, and we have about four months of expenses saved. There are some other factories nearby. A small software change would leave our mortgage plan as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep feeding wire through the drawing machine and measuring the first spool with the lead. I use AI now and then to explain a fault code, but I check the manual before touching a tension setting. We'll add a new amount from each full pay month to savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The line pays, the household works, and I can get better at the trade by doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a fault answer wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week an AI answer suggested a motor fault, but the lead found a rough guide wheel. We changed the wheel and the next spool measured correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do you add to savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are eight and fourteen, so the mortgage is only one line on the budget. My partner and I set aside money after school costs and groceries, not before the bills are known.

say: **AI invoices** may be quicker while spokes still need physical diameter checks.
The **wire crew** should measure each first spool after a setting change.
think: Two **steady wages** and four months saved keep the mortgage covered now.
Some nearby **factory jobs** provide backup if this line changes.
do: **Keep** feeding wire and measuring the first spool.
**Add** new savings from full wages after school and food costs.
feel: **Calm** about current paid work and modest AI gains.
S0.quote: A thin spoke is not fixed by a better spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Aaron already uses **AI occasionally** for fault words but relies on the machine manual and gauge.
His **moderate reserve** and two regular wages make this mild outcome secure.

steps.text: Keep drawing bicycle-spoke wire and measuring first spools
Add new savings from full wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the supplier has every reason to use a faster invoicing system, but it ought to train the people who know the customers. At my plant I want a proper paid test before any new wire schedule replaces the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner enters invoices for a plumbing supplier, and much of that work is exactly what AI can do first. If those hours shrink, our four-month reserve buys time but not a second wage. The spoke line itself still needs hands, so I expect my factory pay to continue for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner will ask the supplier for a written hours plan. I'll request a paid supervised session on the plant's new AI wire-order screen; if offered, I'll learn how to correct an order against actual spool use. We will hold off replacing the kitchen table until we know whether the invoice wage changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a realistic cut to one household wage, though I can learn a proven tool and keep working. A faster invoice is no comfort if the person who checks it loses paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the wire-order screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enter the last three spool weights and compare the new order with what the machine actually used. If it orders too little wire, the lead should see the correction before production starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why postpone the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our table is scratched, not broken, so waiting is easy. If my partner's paid hours are actually reduced, the money goes to the mortgage and food instead of furniture.

say: **AI invoicing** may save supplier time but put customer clerks at risk.
The **wire plant** should test new orders against measured spool use.
think: My partner's **invoice hours** could shrink before robots reach my line.
Four months of **savings** give time but cannot replace long-term wages.
do: **Ask** supplier for a written invoice-hours plan.
**Learn** AI wire-order corrections if paid supervised session offered.
**Postpone** kitchen-table replacement while partner pay is uncertain.
S1.quote: A faster invoice is no comfort if the person who checks it loses paid hours.
fieldNote: His **household risk** comes from a partner’s directly exposed invoice work, not immediate spoke automation.
The **screen lesson remains conditional** on an offered paid supervised session beyond his existing fault-code queries.

steps.text: Ask plumbing supplier for written invoice-clerk hours plan
Learn AI wire-order correction if paid supervised place offered
Postpone kitchen-table replacement until invoice hours are confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028 could do the supplier's invoicing, and capable robots around 2031 could draw, straighten and inspect spokes. I'd tell our family that paid apprenticeships need to start before either wage falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my partner's invoice hours to be cut sharply, and the robot could later take the simple wire-feeding tasks I still do. Four months saved won't carry two missing wages and a mortgage for long. I have lain awake deciding which child cost we'd delay first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week we'll request written hours plans from both workplaces. If the supplier cuts my partner's wage, I'll apply to posted local machine jobs with safe duties and enough regular pay, while keeping my current shift. If the plant offers a funded, paid-time practical maintenance apprenticeship on a guarded wire line, I'll enrol only when a real place is offered; after qualifying and if my own hours fall, I'll apply to posted local maintenance posts with safe duties at bill-covering pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a major household pay loss, despite four months saved. I can work and learn, but I cannot promise a factory will offer a place before the supplier cuts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the apprenticeship teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to isolate the wire drawbench, release tension safely and gauge a test spool with the trainer beside me. A video of a clean spool would not teach safe wire-drawbench isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would family help make another shift possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother could take the children after school if I had a real paid late shift. I would ask only after seeing the posted hours and rate. Family help cannot make a low wage cover the mortgage.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may cut invoicing before robots draw spokes around 2031.
Families need **paid practical apprenticeships** before both wages are at risk.
think: A sharp **invoice-pay cut** and later wire-line loss could threaten our mortgage.
Four months of **savings** cannot bridge two wages indefinitely.
do: **Request** written hours plans from both workplaces this week.
**Apply** to posted safe local machine jobs after partner pay falls, at sufficient pay.
**Enrol** in guarded maintenance apprenticeship only if a real funded paid place provides a trainer beside me.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major pay loss and sleepless household worry.
S2.quote: A video of a clean spool would not teach safe wire-drawbench isolation.
fieldNote: He expects **partner invoice cuts** by the thinking-AI date and physical line risk around 2031.
The apprenticeship and two **job applications** have distinct triggers, safety, qualification and adequate posted pay.

steps.text: Apply for posted safe local machine role if partner wage cut, pay sufficient
Enrol in guarded maintenance apprenticeship only if funded paid place includes a trainer
Apply for posted safe local maintenance role if qualified, own hours cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI takes supplier invoices in 2031 and capable robots draw spokes around 2034, I'd tell the plant five years is enough for adult apprenticeships. A promise to retrain workers is useful only when a wage comes with the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the invoice change and 51 when robots can handle the wire line. The children and mortgage will still cost money. I have time to gain a maintenance skill while my operator wage is coming in, but I cannot assume the supplier will keep every desk shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep drawing spokes and save new money from full pay months after bills. If the plant offers a recognized maintenance course with covered fees, paid release and guarded drawbench practice, I'll enrol this year. After qualifying, if either wage falls, I'll apply to posted local maintenance jobs only where safe duties, regular hours and base pay cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household wages, though the longer lead lets me train without abandoning the current shift. I want the certificate to point to an actual local job, not sit in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real assessment include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assessment should include locking the drawbench, changing a worn guide and measuring the first ten spokes. I would want a qualified setter to sign each step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you assess a job posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted base rate with our mortgage, food and school costs. A fine title with uncertain overtime is not a pay plan.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes supplier invoicing before robots draw spokes around 2034.
Adult **paid apprenticeships** can protect skills before physical work changes.
think: At **51**, our mortgage may still need both wages.
A **recognized certificate** helps only with an adequate posted local opening.
do: **Keep** drawing spokes and add new savings after bills.
**Enrol** in recognized maintenance training if funded paid guarded place offered.
**Apply** to posted local maintenance if qualified, household wage cut, pay sufficient.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household pay loss, with time to train.
S3.quote: A fine title with uncertain overtime is not a pay plan.
fieldNote: He keeps **new saving** separate from the existing four-month reserve.
Training requires **offered funded paid practice**; the later application requires qualification, a real safe posting and adequate base pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full wire-line wages after bills
Enrol in recognized maintenance course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local maintenance if qualified, wage cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could take invoice work, and capable robots around 2039 could draw and inspect spokes. I'd tell my children that work changes, but practical teaching and looking after family still matter across the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the supplier invoicing changes and 56 when the robot reaches physical wire work. Our children will be older, but I expect to keep earning. Four months saved gives us choices now, and ten years of wages could make a stronger reserve if jobs hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the paid wire shift and add fresh savings from full months. I'll ask the lead about a funded, paid-time maintenance place with guarded practice and enrol if one is actually offered. Each year we'll check posted local roles; if the invoice wage or my line hours later fall, I'll apply after qualifying only for safe work with enough stated regular pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later change while our own two wages seem secure today. I can wait to see which equipment works before investing time in a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a robot drawbench on a closed line, with a worker at the stop and ten spokes checked by gauge. A neat screen is not evidence that a spoke will hold its tension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children to ask a working adult to show them a trade before paying for a course. I won't promise that one craft is robot-proof; I can show them how to check a real part.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes invoices before robots draw spokes around 2039.
A **safe robot trial** should include a stop worker and real gauge checks.
think: At **56**, I expect to need factory wages beyond the robot date.
Four months of **savings** can grow only if full paid work continues.
do: **Continue** the wire shift and add new wage savings.
**Enrol** in funded guarded maintenance training if paid place offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local work if qualified, later wages fall, pay sufficient.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work while current household pay remains secure.
S4.quote: A neat screen is not evidence that a spoke will hold its tension.
fieldNote: He follows a **proven-first route** while protecting current household wages and future savings.
The later **application** needs an offered qualification, actual wage reduction and adequate safe local posting.

steps.text: Save new money from full wire-line wages after bills
Enrol in maintenance course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local role if qualified, wages fall, pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because my partner's invoice wage could shrink before robots reach my wire line around 2031. A real funded paid maintenance apprenticeship and a posted safe local job with regular pay enough for our mortgage would help us keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who measures the first spoke after a robot changes the guide wheel. A wire spool can look neat while every spoke is a shade too thin.

headlineQuote: A wire spool can look neat while every spoke is a shade too thin.
portrait: **Aaron**, 43, is a junior wire-drawing operator with secondary school education and typical factory pay.
He and his invoice-clerk partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with four months saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for fault words and waits for proven paid lessons before learning new controls.
His **traditional outlook** favors paid practical apprenticeships and family support as both jobs face different automation dates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his partner’s invoice hours before robots threaten the spoke line around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded paid apprenticeship** and a posted safe local job at sufficient regular pay would help protect their mortgage.
